name: Colin Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Colin. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollin Bank, which is a co-op farm, owned by about forty member families, with a manager called Rachel running it day to day. I start at six with the pigs, two hundred sows, feeding, checking for lame ones, moving weaners, and then in the season I'm on the potato harvester or grading line. I came over from driving a forklift in a warehouse two years ago, so I'm still the new lad at forty-three, which is funny.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you switch, and how's it gone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The warehouse put in a scanning system that timed your every move, and I hated being a dot on a screen. Here I'm outdoors and I can see the point of what I do. It's gone all right, though I still get things wrong with the farrowing pens, and my partner Ana, who's a nurse, laughs that I came home from a warehouse to a pig shed and call it promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, it was never going to milk a sow. At the co-op meeting I'd say good, now we can stop worrying and get on. Online I don't say much, I just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays my job, and Ana's job at the hospital stays hers, and that feels secure. We've got about four months put by, the mortgage is manageable on two wages. In a world where AI is mostly hype, the pigs still need feeding at six and that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, basically. I'd finish the forklift-to-telehandler ticket the co-op is paying for, and keep using the chat thing now and then when I'm stuck on a pig problem at night. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit flat maybe, after all the fuss, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you came from a warehouse that timed you. Does that history shape how you see AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. The warehouse system did make me faster, but it was the bosses who took the gain, not us. Technology doesn't scare me; who owns the technology is what scares me. Here at least the farm belongs to people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about the next few years, even in a quiet world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pig prices, swine fever, the usual farm stuff. If a disease outbreak hit, the co-op would have to cull and I'd be on short hours. But that's farming, not AI, and Rachel has always been straight with us.

say: I'd say AI was **never going** to milk a sow or feed one.
At the **co-op meeting** I'd say we can stop worrying and get on.
think: My job and Ana's **nursing job** both stay as they are, which feels secure.
With about **four months** saved and two wages, the mortgage is manageable.
do: Finish the **telehandler ticket** the co-op is paying for this winter.
Keep using the **chat tool** now and then for pig problems at night.
feel: **Calm**, if a bit flat after all the fuss about AI.
S0.quote: Technology doesn't scare me; who owns the technology is what scares me.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **two steady wages** and a co-op employer he trusts.
The warehouse taught him that **ownership** of technology matters more than the technology.
His only background worry is **disease outbreaks**, a farming risk, not an AI one.

steps.text: Finish the co-op-funded telehandler ticket this winter
Ask the chat tool about pig health problems when stuck at night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming for office work first and farms later, so we've got a head start to plan. At the co-op I'd stand up and say any machine we buy should cut hours, not jobs. Online I'd share the stuff about a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, probably not much for a few years, because the hands-on side is slow. But Rachel's spreadsheets, the feed ordering, the potato contracts, that's the thinking work and it goes first. Then the savings get spent on something, and I'd want a say in what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the feed planning tool properly once Rachel has it running, maybe two evenings a month. I'd put my name up for the co-op's workers' committee. And I'd start adding another fifty a month to savings, just because.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Interested, really, as long as it's done fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said who owns it matters. How would that play out at Hollin Bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're forty families and the workers get a vote on big buys. If someone wants to spend money on a robot, it goes to the meeting. At a co-op farm, a robot that cuts my hours could also be a robot that gives me Fridays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rachel's job look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less typing, more walking the fields, I'd hope. She's good with the animals and she's stuck at a desk half the week. If the AI does her paperwork, she might actually teach me the farrowing properly.

say: I'd say office work goes first and farms later, so we have a **head start**.
At the co-op I'd argue new machines should **cut hours**, not jobs.
think: My hands-on work changes slowly, but **Rachel's paperwork** and feed ordering go first.
The money saved gets spent somewhere, and I want **a say** in where.
do: Learn the **feed planning tool** once Rachel sets it up, two evenings a month.
Add **£50 a month** to our savings.
feel: **Uneasy** but more interested than frightened, if it's done fairly.
S1.quote: At a co-op farm, a robot that cuts my hours could also be a robot that gives me Fridays off.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking work** on the farm going first and his own work later.
His progressive views show in a hope for a **shorter week** rather than fewer jobs.
Steady adopter: he'd learn tools **once Rachel** has them running.

steps.text: Learn the feed planning tool once the manager has it running
Stand for the workers' committee at the co-op farm
Put an extra £50 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules, now, and the profits have to be shared out. At the co-op I'd push for a plan before 2031, not after. Online I'd probably get into arguments, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 I'm in trouble. The 2028 part barely touches my sheds, but the robots three years later can do my job, and I'm not the best at it. I'd have three years to find a place that still needs people, and I don't know what that place is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd sign up for the robot maintenance course at the agricultural college, evenings, because someone will have to fix the things. I'd move savings up to a hundred a month and cancel the second car. And I'd push the co-op to write down what happens to workers before any machine is bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. There's a knot in my stomach thinking about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about the co-op voting. Would forty families vote to keep you on if a robot could do your work cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. They're decent people, but they've got their own mortgages, and if a robot sow-feeder is half my wage they'd feel the pressure. I'd rather be the co-op worker who fixes the robot than the one the robot made redundant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ana's work at the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana thinks nursing is safe because you can't automate holding someone's hand. Her charting and drug rounds might change in 2028, but the hands-on care is later. That's what keeps our house afloat in my head, her wage.

At the co-op I'd push for a **plan before 2031**, not after.
think: The 2028 part barely touches my sheds, but **robots by 2031** can do my job.
Ana's **hospital wage** is what keeps our house afloat in my head.
do: Sign up for the evening **robot maintenance** course at the agricultural college.
Raise savings to **£100 a month** and sell the second car.

feel: **Worried** properly, with a knot in his stomach about 2031.

fieldNote: He grasps that the **three-year gap** is his window to move into a new role.
His plan is to become **the one who fixes** the robots rather than be replaced.
Ana's **nursing income** gives him a sense of control, which keeps him from alarm.

steps.text: Start the evening robot maintenance course at the agricultural college
Sell the second car and save £100 a month
Push the co-op to put worker protections in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, just calmer. I'd say we've got time to get this right, and I'd keep banging on at the co-op about sharing the gains. I'd also say, quietly, that people like me need training paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me until about 2034 on the hands-on side, which is eight years. That's enough to finish the robot maintenance course without killing myself doing it in a hurry. I'd still lose the pig job as it is now, but I might have the next one ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the college course over two years instead of one. I'd ask Rachel to let me shadow whoever services the feed system now. And I'd stay on the workers' committee to get a retraining fund written into the co-op rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but in a way I can work with. Less of a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years instead of two change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jakub to learn things where you're working with people or fixing things that break. I'd tell my son that the safest job is the one where you're the person the machine calls when it's stuck. He wants to be a footballer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jakub, who's fourteen, about choosing a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And Lena's only nine, she'll be fine, she's cleverer than both of us.

I'd say quietly that people like me need **training paid for**.
think: Hands-on work holds until about **2034**, eight years from now.

fieldNote: More time turns his plan from a sprint into a **steady route**, but the job loss stays.

His advice to Jakub centres on being **the person** machines call for help.

steps.text: Take the robot maintenance course over two years of evenings
Shadow the technician who services the co-op's feed system
Get a retraining fund written into the co-op's rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we don't waste it. At the co-op I'd say let's plan the robots in, together, and keep everyone. Online I'd still be the bloke sharing articles about the four-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it means I'd likely make it. By 2039 I'd have a trade in machines, or I'd be a senior stockman on a farm that still keeps some people. And Ana would be near her pension. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course properly and get a second ticket, maybe electrics. I'd keep learning the farm software as it comes in, slowly, like I always do. And I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each year so it's smaller by the time anything lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe, but mostly fine. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-six by 2039. Does ten years feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's long enough for a forty-three-year-old who's willing to learn. If it were two years I'd be scrambling, but ten years is two courses and a bit of luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with the money in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overpay the mortgage, like I said, maybe an extra hundred a month. Paying off the house early is the one robot-proof thing a pig man can buy.

At the co-op I'd say plan the robots in **together** and keep everyone.
think: By **2039** I'd likely have a trade in machines or a senior farm role.
Ana would be **near her pension**, so the household is steadier.

S4.quote: Paying off the house early is the one robot-proof thing a pig man can buy.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **steady pace** work in his favour.

steps.text: Finish the maintenance course and add an electrics ticket
Learn each new piece of farm software as the co-op adopts it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years after that the robots are in the pig sheds and I'm only halfway through learning anything else. What would help is paid retraining, evenings or day release, and a rule that co-ops and farms share the savings with the workers who get moved. A robot on a co-op farm should mean a shorter week for the workers, not a shorter list of workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be new at forty-three. I'm still learning this job, and now I'm being told to learn the next one. It's a lot, but I'd rather be told early.

headlineQuote: A robot on a co-op farm should mean a shorter week for the workers, not a shorter list of workers.
portrait: Colin is a **junior stockman** at Hollin Bank, a co-op farm, after leaving a warehouse job.
His partner Ana's **nursing wage** and about four months' savings make him feel steady.
He picks up tools **once proven** and plans to retrain in robot maintenance.
His politics focus on **who owns** the machines and sharing gains.
He moves from calm to **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures, then eases with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach his pig sheds before he'd finished retraining.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that farms **share savings** from robots with workers.
